lec05kp11en-u01-p1-card1.name: term:Pruning
lec05kp11en-u01-p1-card1.text: **Pruning**: Pruning removes connections or units to reduce adjustable structure; performance must be checked afterward.

lec05kp11en-u01-p1-card2.name: u01-p1-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p1-card2.text: Start with one connection: setting its weight to zero removes its contribution to the score.

lec05kp11en-u01-p1-card3.name: u01-p1-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p1-card3.text: The goal is acceptable loss and held-out performance with a simpler model, not deletion for its own sake.

lec05kp11en-u01-p2-title.text: Zeroing a weight changes it by its negative

lec05kp11en-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-curvature
lec05kp11en-u01-p2-fig1.text: 局部二次損失：小權重A刪除代價2，大權重B刪除代價0.01。

image.alt: Two exact quadratic local loss profiles: deleting weight A costs two, while deleting larger weight B costs 0.01.

lec05kp11en-u01-p2-card1.name: u01-p2-card1
lec05kp11en-u01-p2-card1.text: w_i is weight i and $\delta w_i$ its change. Since $w_i+\delta w_i=0$, deletion uses $\delta w_i=-w_i$.

lec05kp11en-u01-p2-card2.name: u01-p2-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p2-card2.text: J is the training objective; $\Delta J$ is its value after deletion minus before deletion. It is not the weight magnitude.

lec05kp11en-u01-p2-card3.name: u01-p2-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p2-card3.text: If $w_i=0.2$, deletion adds $-0.2$. A small parameter change need not have a small effect.

lec05kp11en-u01-p3-title.text: Steeper loss curvature can make a small change costly

lec05kp11en-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp11en-u01-p3-bridge.text: A small parameter change need not have a small effect. Which feature of the loss curve measures that sensitivity?

lec05kp11en-u01-p3-next-question.name: u01-p3-next-question
lec05kp11en-u01-p3-next-question.text: How can local slopes and curvature estimate a deletion cost?

lec05kp11en-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-curvature
lec05kp11en-u01-p3-fig1.text: 局部二次損失：小權重A刪除代價2，大權重B刪除代價0.01。

image.alt: Two exact quadratic local loss profiles: deleting weight A costs two, while deleting larger weight B costs 0.01.

lec05kp11en-u01-p3-card1.name: term:Curvature
lec05kp11en-u01-p3-card1.text: **Curvature**: Local curvature describes how quickly the loss slope changes; here it is measured by a second derivative.

lec05kp11en-u01-p3-card2.name: term:Hessian
lec05kp11en-u01-p3-card2.text: **Hessian**: The Hessian matrix H collects second partial derivatives; $H_{ii}$ measures curvature in weight direction i.

lec05kp11en-u01-p3-card3.name: u01-p3-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p3-card3.text: Weight A is smaller but lies in a more curved loss profile; its deletion can cost more than deleting larger weight B.

lec05kp11en-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp11en-u01-p4-title.text: Near a minimum, second-order terms estimate deletion cost

lec05kp11en-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp11en-u01-p4-bridge.text: The Hessian matrix collects curvature in weight directions. How can local slopes and curvature estimate a deletion cost?

lec05kp11en-u01-p4-next-question.name: u01-p4-next-question
lec05kp11en-u01-p4-next-question.text: Which of weight A and weight B should go first?

lec05kp11en-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-curvature
lec05kp11en-u01-p4-fig1.text: 局部二次損失：小權重A刪除代價2，大權重B刪除代價0.01。

image.alt: Two exact quadratic local loss profiles: deleting weight A costs two, while deleting larger weight B costs 0.01.

lec05kp11en-u01-p4-card1.name: u01-p4-card1
lec05kp11en-u01-p4-card1.text: $\Delta J\approx\sum_i g_i\delta w_i+\frac12\sum_{i,j}H_{ij}\delta w_i\delta w_j$, where $g_i=\partial J/\partial w_i$ is the local slope.

lec05kp11en-u01-p4-card2.name: u01-p4-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p4-card2.text: Near a minimum, take $g_i\approx0$. A diagonal approximation drops cross-weight terms, leaving $\Delta J\approx\frac12\sum_iH_{ii}(\delta w_i)^2$.

lec05kp11en-u01-p4-card3.name: term:Saliency
lec05kp11en-u01-p4-card3.text: **Saliency**: Substituting $\delta w_i=-w_i$ gives estimated deletion cost $s_i=\frac12H_{ii}w_i^2$, called saliency. It is an approximation, not measured loss.

lec05kp11en-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp11en-u01-p5-title.text: Deleting smaller weight A costs two hundred times more

lec05kp11en-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp11en-u01-p5-bridge.text: Estimated deletion cost uses both curvature and squared magnitude. Which of weight A and weight B should go first?

lec05kp11en-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-saliency
lec05kp11en-u01-p5-fig1.text: 對數刻度比較兩個可手算的刪除代價2與0.01。

image.alt: Deletion costs two and 0.01 on a logarithmic scale, comparing curvature-based rather than magnitude-only importance.

lec05kp11en-u01-p5-card3.name: u01-p5-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p5-card3.text: Compare: $2/0.01=200$. This local estimate prefers deleting B, despite its larger magnitude.

lec05kp11en-u01-p6-card1.name: u01-p6-card1
lec05kp11en-u01-p6-card1.text: Away from a minimum, the first-order term may matter; a large deletion can also invalidate the local expansion.

lec05kp11en-u01-p6-card2.name: u01-p6-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p6-card2.text: Multiple deletions can interact. Negative Hessian curvature should not be treated as a safe importance score.

lec05kp11en-u01-p6-card3.name: u01-p6-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p6-card3.text: Prune in small steps, measure loss again, retrain the remaining weights and keep the best validation model.

lec05kp11en-u01-p7-card2.text: Stop using validation, an allowed loss increase or a resource budget. A smaller pruned network is not always more accurate.

lec05kp11en-u01-p7-card3.name: u01-p7-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p7-card3.text: Full-Hessian methods can account for compensating changes in other weights, at higher storage and computation cost.

lec05kp11en-u01-p8-card1.name: term:Regularization
lec05kp11en-u01-p8-card1.text: **Regularization**: Regularization adds a model preference or constraint beyond data fit, changing which solutions are favored.

lec05kp11en-u01-p8-card2.name: u01-p8-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p8-card2.text: $J_{\mathrm{total}}=J_{\mathrm{data}}+\alpha P(\mathbf w)$. The first term measures data error; P penalizes weights and $\alpha\ge0$ sets its strength.

lec05kp11en-u01-p8-card3.name: u01-p8-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p8-card3.text: Summed and averaged data losses have different scales, so the same numerical alpha has different effects.

lec05kp11en-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp11en-u01-p9-title.text: A slightly worse fit can have a better penalized objective

lec05kp11en-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp11en-u01-p9-bridge.text: Regularization adds a model preference beyond data fit. How does a weight penalty change the comparison between two candidates?

lec05kp11en-u01-p9-card1.text: Model A has data loss $0.10$ and penalty $4$; B has data loss $0.20$ and penalty $1$. Fix $\alpha=0.1$.

lec05kp11en-u01-p9-card3.name: u01-p9-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p9-card3.text: With $\alpha=0$, A wins. Select alpha with validation data; lower penalized training objective need not imply lower test error.

lec05kp11en-u01-p10-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-rho
lec05kp11en-u01-p10-fig1.text: 飽和懲罰 w平方除以1加w平方；w為0.2、1、3時約0.0385、0.5、0.9。

image.alt: Saturating penalty w squared divided by one plus w squared; marked values at 0.2, one and three.

lec05kp11en-u01-p10-card1.name: term:Saturating penalty
lec05kp11en-u01-p10-card1.text: **Saturating penalty**: $\rho(w)=w^2/(\tau^2+w^2)$ with scale $\tau>0$ approaches 1 for large magnitude weights.

lec05kp11en-u01-p10-card3.name: u01-p10-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p10-card3.text: Compare magnitudes: $|w|\ll\tau$ describes the near-zero range, not a signed comparison between w and tau.

lec05kp11en-u01-p11-title.text: Smooth shrinkage is not the same as exact deletion

lec05kp11en-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp11en-u01-p11-bridge.text: A saturating penalty approaches one for large magnitude weights and is small near zero. Does smooth shrinkage give exact deletion?

lec05kp11en-u01-p11-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-gradient
lec05kp11en-u01-p11-fig1.text: 飽和懲罰的導數，在零點為零；因此平滑懲罰本身不會保證精確零權重。

image.alt: Derivative of the smooth saturating penalty, zero at the origin, which does not guarantee finite-step exact deletion.

lec05kp11en-u01-p11-card1.name: u01-p11-card1
lec05kp11en-u01-p11-card1.text: $\rho'(w)=2\tau^2w/(\tau^2+w^2)^2$. Its derivative is zero at $w=0$; finite updates need not reach exact zero.

lec05kp11en-u01-p11-card2.name: term:Weight elimination
lec05kp11en-u01-p11-card2.text: **Weight elimination**: Weight elimination encourages shrinkage and periodically zeroes or removes weights below a chosen threshold.

lec05kp11en-u01-p11-card3.name: u01-p11-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p11-card3.text: Use $|w_i|<\varepsilon$ for deletion. Epsilon is a deletion threshold; tau is the penalty scale. Their roles differ.

lec05kp11en-u01-p12-card1.text: The source also discusses penalties on neuron outputs, encouraging some units to respond less rather than scoring only individual connections.

lec05kp11en-u01-p12-card2.name: u01-p12-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p12-card2.text: A small unit output may be amplified by a large downstream weight. Inspect the path and performance after removal.

lec05kp11en-u01-p12-card3.name: u01-p12-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p12-card3.text: Connection deletion, unit deletion and numerical shrinkage are distinct operations and should be recorded separately.

lec05kp11en-u01-p13-card1.text: The source cites a two-layer sigmoid-network result whose complexity term includes $A^3\sqrt{\log d/N}$ under training-error and weight-norm conditions.

lec05kp11en-u01-p13-card2.name: u01-p13-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p13-card2.text: A bounds each unit's sum of absolute weights; d is input dimension and N sample count. This is the source's scaling summary, not a complete probability bound.

lec05kp11en-u01-p13-card3.name: u01-p13-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p13-card3.text: With d and N fixed, doubling A multiplies this term by $2^3=8$. The term is not itself a classification error probability.

lec05kp11en-u01-p14-card1.text: **Residual**: The residual is target minus prediction, $e_n=t_n-\hat y_n$, with n indexing examples.

lec05kp11en-u01-p14-card2.name: term:Cascade correlation
lec05kp11en-u01-p14-card2.text: **Cascade correlation**: Cascade correlation adds a hidden unit responsive to current residuals, then refits output weights.

lec05kp11en-u01-p14-card3.name: u01-p14-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p14-card3.text: The new unit receives original inputs and earlier hidden outputs. Train its incoming weights, then freeze them.

lec05kp11en-u01-p15-card1.text: A single-output teaching score is $S=|\sum_n(v_n-\bar v)(e_n-\bar e)|$, where bars denote sample means.

lec05kp11en-u01-p15-card2.name: u01-p15-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p15-card2.text: For $e=(-1,1)$, candidate $v=(-1,1)$ gives $S=|-1\times(-1)+1\times1|=2$. Constant $v=(1,1)$ centers to zero and gives $S=0$.

lec05kp11en-u01-p15-card3.text: After selecting the candidate and freezing incoming weights, refit outgoing weights for squared error. S is unnormalized, not a Pearson coefficient.

lec05kp11en-u01-p19-bridge.text: The original figure shows a wavy boundary becoming approximately straight with twenty-five weights. How is a plotted decision boundary obtained?

lec05kp11en-u01-p19-next-question.text: Returning to deletion costs, what changes when other weights may compensate?

lec05kp11en-u01-p19-fig1.text: 補充計分r=x2-0.6x1-1的logistic輸出，其0.5等高線由401乘401網格計算；不是訓練實驗。

image.alt: An illustrative logistic score r=x2-0.6*x1-1 has a 0.5 contour calculated on a 401-by-401 grid; this is not a fitted source network.

lec05kp11en-u01-p19-card1.name: u01-p19-card1
lec05kp11en-u01-p19-card1.text: Added illustration: use score $r=x_2-0.6x_1-1$ and continuous response $p=1/(1+e^{-r})$, thresholded at 0.5. This is not the source's trained model.

lec05kp11en-u01-p19-card2.name: u01-p19-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p19-card2.text: Evaluate p on a 2-D grid and draw the $p=0.5$ contour. It is the thresholded class that switches between 0 and 1.

lec05kp11en-u01-p19-card3.name: u01-p19-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p19-card3.text: Record grid resolution, threshold and coordinate range. A smoother figure alone is not an accuracy comparison.

lec05kp11en-u01-p20-title.text: Extension: full curvature lets other weights compensate

lec05kp11en-u01-p20-bridge.name: u01-p20-bridge
lec05kp11en-u01-p20-bridge.text: A smoother figure is not an accuracy comparison. Returning to deletion costs, what changes when other weights may compensate?

lec05kp11en-u01-p20-next-question.name: u01-p20-next-question
lec05kp11en-u01-p20-next-question.text: Can you now rank candidates and evaluate a saturating penalty?

lec05kp11en-u01-p20-card1.name: u01-p20-card1
lec05kp11en-u01-p20-card1.text: In an added quadratic example, $H=\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ and deleting $w_1=0.5$ gives $\delta w_1=-0.5$.

lec05kp11en-u01-p20-card2.name: u01-p20-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p20-card2.text: Fixing $\delta w_2=0$ costs $\frac12\times4\times0.5^2=0.5$. Allowing compensation gives $\Delta J=0.5-0.5\delta w_2+(\delta w_2)^2$.

lec05kp11en-u01-p20-card3.name: u01-p20-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p20-card3.text: Differentiating gives $-0.5+2\delta w_2=0$, so $\delta w_2=0.25$. Cost $0.5-0.125+0.0625=0.4375$ is below 0.5.

lec05kp11en-u01-p21-title.name: u01-p21-title
lec05kp11en-u01-p21-title.text: Extension: rank deletion candidates and evaluate a penalty

lec05kp11en-u01-p21-bridge.name: u01-p21-bridge
lec05kp11en-u01-p21-bridge.text: Compensating changes lowered the quadratic cost from 0.5 to 0.4375. Can you now rank candidates and evaluate a saturating penalty?

image.alt: The practice penalty uses tau two: w squared divided by four plus w squared.

lec05kp11en-u01-p21-card1.name: u01-p21-card1
lec05kp11en-u01-p21-card1.text: Question 1: C has weight 0.5 and curvature 8; D has weight 2 and curvature 0.1. Which has lower saliency $s=Hw^2/2$?

lec05kp11en-u01-p21-card2.name: u01-p21-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p21-card2.text: Question 2: set $\tau=2,w=2$ and calculate $\rho(w)$. Does that value mean the weight has been deleted?

lec05kp11en-u01-p22-title.name: u01-p22-title
lec05kp11en-u01-p22-title.text: Extension: delete D first; a half penalty is not deletion

lec05kp11en-u01-p22-bridge.name: u01-p22-bridge
lec05kp11en-u01-p22-bridge.text: Question 1 compares C and D using saliency; question 2 distinguishes a penalty from deletion. What do the numbers give?

lec05kp11en-u01-p22-next-question.name: u01-p22-next-question
lec05kp11en-u01-p22-next-question.text: Can you recompute an example and state its limits?

lec05kp11en-u01-p22-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp11-saliency-practice
lec05kp11en-u01-p22-fig1.text: 練習C與D的顯著度為1與0.2，與同頁解答一致。

image.alt: Practice C and D have saliencies one and 0.2, matching the worked answer.

lec05kp11en-u01-p22-card1.name: u01-p22-card1
lec05kp11en-u01-p22-card1.text: Question 1: $s_C=\frac12\times8\times0.5^2=1$; $s_D=\frac12\times0.1\times2^2=0.2$. The estimate favors deleting D.

lec05kp11en-u01-p22-card2.name: u01-p22-card2
lec05kp11en-u01-p22-card2.text: Question 2: $\rho(2)=2^2/(2^2+2^2)=4/8=0.5$. The weight remains 2 until an explicit zeroing or removal operation.

lec05kp11en-u01-p22-card3.name: u01-p22-card3
lec05kp11en-u01-p22-card3.text: Check the lesson: a larger weight can have lower saliency. Next ask whether connections can share fewer parameters from the start.

steps.label: Pruning
steps.speakerNotes: Level: third-year undergraduate. Intended for self-study outside the 270-minute class.

steps.label: Delete with care
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Self-study entry.
Removing a branch of a circuit may affect the whole system. Line thickness alone is not importance; a small weight can matter more.
Next page: Pruning sets a connection weight to zero. What parameter change describes removing its contribution to the score?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 1: Ask the cost before deleting a connection.

steps.label: Deletion amount
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Ask the cost before deleting a connection.
Delta denotes a finite change here, not a backpropagated error signal. Compute the deletion amount before looking at the loss curvature.
Next page: A small parameter change need not have a small effect. Which feature of the loss curve measures that sensitivity?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 2: Zeroing a weight changes it by its negative.

steps.label: Curvature matters
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Zeroing a weight changes it by its negative.
These are two exact local quadratic examples, not two points on one curve. Find each minimum, then move to weight zero.
Next page: The Hessian matrix collects curvature in weight directions. How can local slopes and curvature estimate a deletion cost?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 3: Steeper loss curvature can make a small change costly.

steps.label: Estimate saliency
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Steeper loss curvature can make a small change costly.
State both assumptions. For a single changed weight with all others fixed, only its diagonal quadratic term remains; coupling matters for joint changes or compensation.
Next page: Estimated deletion cost uses both curvature and squared magnitude. Which of weight A and weight B should go first?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 4: Near a minimum, second-order terms estimate deletion cost.

steps.label: Small but important
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Near a minimum, second-order terms estimate deletion cost.
Do not read log-scale bar heights as linear ratios. The exact quadratic example verifies a principle, not a universal factor of two hundred.
Next page: Deleting smaller weight A costs two hundred times more in the local estimate. When is the approximation unreliable?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 5: Deleting smaller weight A costs two hundred times more.

steps.label: Local limits
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Deleting smaller weight A costs two hundred times more.
Record predicted and measured loss changes side by side. A discrepancy should trigger a review of assumptions rather than cosmetic smoothing.
Next page: Multiple deletions can interact, so prune in small steps and measure loss again. How should the full loop work?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 6: Saliency is local: remeasure and retrain after deletion.

steps.label: Pruning loop
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Saliency is local: remeasure and retrain after deletion.
Ask where the loop returns after an unacceptable validation result and when a model is saved. A reported checking interval is a case setting, not a universal constant.
Next page: Pruning alternates selective deletion, retraining and validation. Can the training objective itself charge for unnecessary structure?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 7: Pruning alternates retraining and selective deletion.

steps.label: Add a penalty
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Pruning alternates retraining and selective deletion.
Regularization need not delete connections; it may retain them with different magnitudes. Fix the data-loss scale before comparing candidates.
Next page: Regularization adds a model preference beyond data fit. How does a weight penalty change the comparison between two candidates?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 8: Penalize unnecessary weights during fitting.

steps.label: Compare objectives
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Penalize unnecessary weights during fitting.
Separate the data-loss column from the total-objective column. Comparing fixed candidates does not prove that an optimizer will find them.
Next page: The penalized objective favored model B despite its higher data loss. What penalty shape does the source use?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 9: A slightly worse fit can have a better penalized objective.

steps.label: Saturating penalty
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: A slightly worse fit can have a better penalized objective.
The source scale w0 is renamed tau to avoid confusion with a bias. A small penalty does not mean a connection has already been deleted.
Next page: A saturating penalty approaches one for large magnitude weights and is small near zero. Does smooth shrinkage give exact deletion?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 10: A saturating penalty treats small and large weights differently.

steps.label: Threshold deletion
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: A saturating penalty treats small and large weights differently.
This saturating penalty is smooth and nonconvex; do not import general convex-optimization guarantees. Validate deletions and record thresholds and actual counts.
Next page: Weight elimination uses a chosen threshold and explicit deletion. Is one small weight enough reason to remove a whole hidden unit?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 11: Smooth shrinkage is not the same as exact deletion.

steps.label: Remove a unit
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Smooth shrinkage is not the same as exact deletion.
Use a volume control followed by an amplifier to illustrate scale compensation; the analogy concerns amplitude, not a claim that the network is linear.
Next page: A small unit output may meet a large downstream weight. Beyond parameter count, can weight magnitudes affect generalization analysis?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 12: Removing a whole unit requires checking its contribution.

steps.label: Weight norms matter
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Removing a whole unit requires checking its contribution.
Constants, confidence parameters and full assumptions are unavailable here. Do not compute a certified error bound from this summary; magnitude and count capture different complexity.
Next page: Weight magnitude and parameter count describe different complexity. Instead of pruning, where should a new hidden unit help a growing network?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 13: Weight magnitude can matter to generalization complexity.

steps.label: Grow for residuals
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Weight magnitude can matter to generalization complexity.
Locate the candidate's incoming and outgoing weights. Growth is more than inserting an arbitrary node.
Next page: The new hidden unit responds to current residuals before its incoming weights freeze. Which objective belongs to each training stage?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 14: Grow a unit where the current model still fails.

steps.label: Freeze then refit
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Grow a unit where the current model still fails.
The two stages optimize different objectives. This single-output illustration does not claim a full reproduction of the original algorithm.
Next page: Cascade correlation separates a residual score from outgoing weights fitted for squared error. What data conditions define the source comparison?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 15: Train incoming weights for residual association, then refit the output.

steps.label: Eight-cluster data
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Train incoming weights for residual association, then refit the output.
Circles and pluses denote classes, not training algorithms. Do not assume the later pruning illustration uses these same samples.
Next page: Eight clusters contribute four hundred training points. With this data design fixed, which network and fitting settings were reported?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 16: The reported simulation has eight clusters and four hundred training points.

steps.label: Reported convergence
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: The reported simulation has eight clusters and four hundred training points.
Preserve the reported values without recommending them for new data. No fabricated timings, accuracies or exact convergence traces are supplied.
Next page: Adaptive momentum was faster in the reported batch case. What did the separate pruning example report about network size?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 17: Faster convergence is a reported case, not a universal ranking.

steps.label: Reported pruning
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Faster convergence is a reported case, not a universal ranking.
The source does not fully specify the counting convention for 480. Do not compare it directly with the previous bias-inclusive count of 20. The plot shows reported counts only.
Next page: The original figure shows a wavy boundary becoming approximately straight with twenty-five weights. How is a plotted decision boundary obtained?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 18: Four hundred eighty to twenty-five is a case result, not a promise.

steps.label: Draw the boundary
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Four hundred eighty to twenty-five is a case result, not a promise.
This clarifies the source's description of output flips without claiming reproduction. A continuous p is not automatically a calibrated probability.
Next page: A smoother figure is not an accuracy comparison. Returning to deletion costs, what changes when other weights may compensate?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 19: Separate a continuous response from a class decision.

steps.label: Extension: coupling
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Separate a continuous response from a class decision.
Positive definiteness gives a unique quadratic minimizer. The example explains compensation without claiming implementation of a complete pruning algorithm.
Next page: Compensating changes lowered the quadratic cost from 0.5 to 0.4375. Can you now rank candidates and evaluate a saturating penalty?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 20: Extension: full curvature lets other weights compensate.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Extension: full curvature lets other weights compensate.
Write the deletion amount before squaring. Equal weight and scale in question 2 test the shape without changing the definition.
Next page: Question 1 compares C and D using saliency; question 2 distinguishes a penalty from deletion. What do the numbers give?
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 21: Extension: rank deletion candidates and evaluate a penalty.

steps.label: Extension: answers
steps.speakerNotes:
Previous page: Extension: rank deletion candidates and evaluate a penalty.
Connect the answers to the earlier misconceptions: magnitude alone is not importance, and a penalty is not deletion. This motivates sharing parameters next.
Next page: Return to the practice and state the assumptions in your own words.
Source: Ch04 KP11, 4.9–4.10; focus 22: Extension: delete D first; a half penalty is not deletion.
